absent: Locking, concurrency, and interrupt-safety rules for mappings, bitmap allocator, and cursor objects.
Exact address discrimination and port derivation used by the dispatch macro, plus ordering and barrier semantics of raw and port primitives.
Complete layouts for cursor backing structures, page, folio, folio queue, vector entries, and PCI device beyond fields observed in use.
Numeric ABI constants, flag encodings, error codes, and width or alignment guarantees beyond the named narrow and wide operations.
Failure-mode contracts for user-access validation, fault allowance, machine-check-safe and cache-aware copies, and wide-operation fallback availability.
Initialisation, teardown, and ownership rules for mappings and IOMMU bitmaps, including allocation, lifetime, and release responsibility.
Behaviour of cross-dossier helpers such as sanitizer checks, warnings, mapping, fault-in, and folio-queue queries whose internals were not routed.

findings.text: Provides narrow device store operations in several widths with native and byte-exchanged variants. Each operation accepts a scalar value plus an abstract I/O address and routes either to a port-based primitive or to a memory-mapped primitive depending on address kind. Exchanged variants reverse byte order before the underlying store so callers observe big-endian layout on the wire.

Provides 64-bit device stores with explicit half ordering. Memory-mapped cases complete as one wide store, optionally byte-exchanged. Port-based cases decompose into two 32-bit stores to adjacent offsets, with low-first/high-first and exchanged orderings offered as distinct operations so drivers can match device sequencing requirements.

Provides repeated and bulk transfers between host buffers and device addresses. Repeated reads/writes move a caller-supplied element count of narrow units, dispatching to string port operations or to looping single-address memory operations. Fixed-width copy helpers move arrays of 32-bit or 64-bit units, with the 64-bit helper degrading to doubled 32-bit moves where wide stores are unavailable.

Provides memory-like bulk operations against I/O mappings: fill a mapping with a repeated byte value, copy from mapping to normal memory, and copy from normal memory to mapping. Implementations progress through leading unaligned bytes, aligned machine-word chunks, and a trailing byte remainder, using raw mapping accesses on the device side and unaligned-safe accesses on the host side where needed.

Exposes a PCI unmapping entry that releases a mapping only when the address denotes a memory-mapped region; port-based addresses require no action. The device argument is accepted for context but does not affect the observed behaviour in these fragments.

Allocates a contiguous run inside a bitmap with alignment and segment-boundary constraints. The allocator searches from a start position for a free run, shifts the start past any run that would straddle a boundary and retries, marks the chosen run occupied, and reports its index; failure is signalled with an all-bits-set return.

Manages a scatter/gather I/O cursor over multiple backing kinds including linear buffers, vector arrays, page vectors, folio queues, arrays and discard sinks. Operations initialise a vector cursor, advance it by consuming bytes and updating remaining length plus segment position, rewind it by restoring length and walking backwards, and report how many bytes remain contiguously available in the current segment.

Moves data to or from the cursor with direction-checked entry points and per-segment callbacks for user versus kernel destinations. Variants cover plain copies, machine-check-safe copies, cache-non-temporal copies, cache-flushing copies, and zero-fill. User-backed transfers additionally allow faulting and validate accessibility, while kernel transfers complete directly and report any shortfall.

Supports page-granular interaction with the cursor: copying whole page ranges to or from the cursor with cross-page continuation, atomically copying from a cursor into a folio with faults disabled, and pre-faulting readable or writable user ranges covered by linear or vector cursors. Other cursor kinds report no pre-fault work.

Device-bound stores validate that source bytes are initialised before they reach hardware, with checked length scaled by element width for repeated operations. Device-sourced loads mark destination bytes initialised after completion, again scaled by width. Single wide and narrow stores apply the same check to the scalar value.

Address kind selects the primitive family: port addresses use port instructions or port string operations, while memory addresses use mapping stores/loads or looping raw accesses at a fixed device address with an advancing host pointer. Repeated-operation counts denote elements rather than bytes, and byte-exchanged narrow stores preserve width while altering order.

Bulk mapping operations align progress to machine-word boundaries and bulk allocator operation respects hardware segment limits. Mapping copies isolate unaligned head/tail bytes from an aligned middle. The bitmap allocator excludes the upper limit from candidacy and restarts search aligned beyond any boundary-straddling candidate before marking occupancy.

Cursor operations maintain remaining byte count, intra-segment offset, segment base and segment remainder consistently. Advance clamps excessive requests to the remaining length and never runs past the end; revert grows the remaining length and restores earlier segments, with vector kinds sharing layout handling. Single-segment queries return the lesser of remaining length and current segment remainder, or zero when exhausted.

Observed cursor state comprises a backing-type discriminator, faulting and direction flags, a remaining byte count, an offset inside the current segment, a segment count, and a type-specific position: base pointer for linear buffers and vectors, page-vector pointer, or folio-queue pointer plus slot. Initialisation establishes vector kind, clears faulting and offset, and records direction, base, segment count and total length.

Cursor lifetime progresses from initialised through partially consumed to exhausted, with optional backward transitions. Advance moves forward across segment boundaries and through chained folio queues; revert moves backward across segment boundaries and chained queues. Discard sinks track only remaining length, while linear kinds track only offset plus length.

Certain cursor and transfer orderings carry failure or device-visibility risks: rewinding a linear or array cursor beyond its recorded start is treated as fatal; wide port stores are observably two separate bus operations whose order callers must choose; pre-fault helpers silently do nothing for backing kinds other than linear and vector, so callers cannot assume pages are resident.

Page and folio transfers validate that offset plus length stays within the identified compound storage before touching data, rejecting oversized requests without progress. Valid transfers split at page boundaries, map one page at a time, advance page and offset together, and stop on completion or shortfall, accumulating bytes actually moved.

Directional entries enforce expected transfer orientation and faulting posture: cursor-to-memory producers require a read-oriented cursor, memory-to-cursor consumers require a write-oriented cursor, and user-backed cursors permit faulting except in explicitly non-faulting or atomic paths where faults are disabled or avoided.
